concepts.title: YAML syntax
concepts.lede: YAML is how most tools are configured: GitHub Actions, Kubernetes, Docker Compose, MLflow. It is just maps, lists and values, held together by indentation.

blocks.x:
# a comment
model:                      # a map (key: value pairs), nested by indenting 2 spaces
  name: distilbert          # text, no quotes needed
  labels: [bug, billing]    # a list, inline style
train:
  epochs: 3                 # a number
  use_gpu: true             # a boolean
  steps:                    # a list, block style: one dash per item
    - load
    - fit
notes: |                    # | keeps line breaks
  first line
  second line

x: **Indentation is structure.** Use spaces, never tabs. Two spaces per level is the convention.
A map is `key: value` (a space after the colon is required). A list item starts with `- `.
`|` keeps newlines in a text block; `>` folds them into one line.

blocks.x: Everything under the same parent must line up exactly. One extra or missing space either changes the meaning or makes the file invalid.

blocks.q: How do you write a list of two items in block style?
choices: `items:` then `- a` and `- b` on their own lines
blocks.why: Each list item gets its own `- ` line, indented under the key.

exercises.prompt: A config file is loaded in Python as `cfg = yaml.safe_load(text)`. What does `cfg["train"]["epochs"] + len(cfg["model"]["labels"])` evaluate to?
hints: Read the number under `train`.
Count the items in the `labels` list.
exercises.code:
model:
  name: distilbert
  labels: [bug, billing, feature]
train:
  epochs: 3
  lr: 0.00002
  use_gpu: true

exercises.prompt: This GitHub Actions snippet is invalid YAML. Which line is the problem?
hints: Look at how far each `- name:` is indented.
The two list items must start in the same column.
Line 4 is one space off.

choices: Indent line 4 by 2 spaces, like line 1's list items
Use a tab instead of spaces

exercises.prompt: Keep the line breaks in this multi-line command.
hints: A single character introduces a literal block.
It looks like a vertical bar.

concepts.title: YAML traps that bite in real projects
concepts.lede: YAML guesses types from how a value looks. Those guesses cause some of the most confusing bugs in CI and config files.

blocks.x:
python-version: 3.10        # loads as the NUMBER 3.1, not the text "3.10"!
python-version: "3.10"      # quote it and it stays text

country: NO                 # PyYAML reads this as the boolean false (the "Norway problem")
country: "NO"               # safe

defaults: &d                # an anchor: name a block
  retries: 3
prod:
  <<: *d                    # merge the anchored block here
  timeout: 30

x: **Quote** anything that could be mistaken for a number, boolean, null or date: versions, `yes`/`no`/`on`/`off`, country codes, zip codes.
Keys must be unique. Duplicates are silently overwritten by many parsers.
Anchors `&name` and aliases `*name` avoid repetition. `<<:` merges a map.

blocks.x: When a pipeline behaves strangely, load the file in Python (`yaml.safe_load`) and print the result. You will see exactly what the tool sees.

blocks.q: You write `python-version: 3.10` in a workflow. Which Python do you get?
blocks.why: YAML reads 3.10 as the number 3.1 and drops the trailing zero. Write `"3.10"`.

exercises.prompt: A workflow contains the line `python-version: 3.10`. What value does `yaml.safe_load` produce for it?
hints: Does the value look like a number?
As a number the trailing zero disappears.
It becomes `3.1`.

explain.ask: In your own words: why does `3.10` turn into `3.1`, and what is the fix?
points: YAML sees an unquoted number and stores it as a float
Quote the value so it stays a string: "3.10"
explain.model: Unquoted, `3.10` is a float, and floats do not keep trailing zeros. Quoting it makes it a string, so the tool receives exactly `3.10`.

exercises.prompt: What does `yaml.safe_load` produce for `country: NO`?
hints: YAML 1.1 treats some words as booleans.
`yes`, `no`, `on` and `off` are among them.
`NO` becomes `False`.

exercises.prompt: The file is meant to describe two settings, but loading it fails. Which line is the problem?
hints: Look at the colon in each line.
A map entry needs a space after the colon.
`version:2` is one text blob, not a key and value.

concepts.title: GitHub Actions: your first workflow
concepts.lede: A workflow is a YAML file in `.github/workflows/`. GitHub runs its jobs on a fresh machine whenever the trigger happens.

blocks.x:
name: CI
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4          # a ready-made step from the marketplace
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt   # a shell command
      - run: pytest -q

rows: named groups of steps; each runs on its own machine
run a reusable action; `with:` passes its inputs

x: A job's steps run in order and share one machine. Separate jobs run in parallel unless one `needs` another.
If any step fails (non-zero exit code), the job stops and the check goes red.

blocks.x: Actions need to download your code first. Almost every job starts with `actions/checkout`.

blocks.q: Which key lists the commands and actions a job runs?

exercises.prompt: Put the lines in order to build a minimal workflow.
hints: `jobs` must come before the job name.
A job's `runs-on` and `steps` are indented under the job name.
`checkout` runs before the tests.

exercises.prompt: Run the workflow on pushes to `main`, on an Ubuntu machine.
hints: The event that fires when commits are pushed.
GitHub's hosted Linux runner has a `-latest` label.
`push` and `ubuntu-latest`.
exercises.template:
on:
  ____:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ____
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: pytest

exercises.prompt: This workflow never starts any job. Which line is the problem?
hints: Check the spelling of each key.

`runs_on` is not recognised.

concepts.title: GitHub Actions: matrix, needs, secrets and caching
concepts.lede: Real pipelines test on several versions, deploy only after tests pass, and keep credentials out of the repo.

blocks.x:
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    strategy:
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest]
        python: ["3.10", "3.11"]        # 2 x 2 = 4 jobs
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: ${{ matrix.python }}
          cache: pip                    # reuse downloaded packages
      - run: pytest -q

  deploy:
    needs: test                          # wait for every test job to pass
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'  # only on main
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: ./deploy.sh
        env:
          AWS_SECRET: ${{ secrets.AWS_SECRET }}   # from Settings > Secrets, never in the file

x: `matrix` multiplies jobs: every combination of its lists runs.
`needs: test` makes a job wait for another and skip if it failed.
`${{ ... }}` is an expression. Secrets are read as `${{ secrets.NAME }}` and are masked in logs.
Add `cache:` or `actions/cache` to avoid re-downloading dependencies on every run.

blocks.x: Never paste credentials into the YAML or print them with `echo`. Store them as repository or environment secrets.

blocks.q: A matrix has `os: [linux, windows]` and `python: ["3.10", "3.11", "3.12"]`. How many jobs run?

exercises.prompt: A matrix defines `os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest]` and `python: ["3.10", "3.11"]`, plus a `deploy` job with `needs: test`. How many `test` jobs run, and when does `deploy` start?
hints: Multiply the list lengths.
`needs` waits for the whole job, which includes every matrix combination.
A single failure stops `deploy`.
choices: 4 jobs; after the first one passes

exercises.prompt: The deploy step cannot authenticate: the token arrives as the literal text `secrets.AWS_TOKEN`. Which line is the problem?
hints: Compare with how expressions are written elsewhere in workflows.
GitHub only evaluates expressions inside `${{ }}`.
Without the braces it is just text.

exercises.prompt: Make `deploy` wait for `test` and run only on the `main` branch.
hints: `needs` takes the name of another job.
The branch name goes at the end of the ref.
`test` and `main`.

concepts.title: Dockerfile basics
concepts.lede: A Dockerfile is a recipe for an image: start from a base, copy in your code, install dependencies, say what to run. A container is a running instance of that image.

blocks.x:
FROM python:3.12-slim              # base image: a small Linux with Python
WORKDIR /app                       # cd into /app (created if missing)
COPY requirements.txt .            # copy a file from your machine into the image
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt   # run a command at BUILD time
COPY . .                           # now copy the rest of the code
EXPOSE 8000                        # documentation: the app listens on 8000
CMD ["uvicorn", "main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]   # run at START time

rows: execute a command and keep the result in the image

x: Build: `docker build -t reviewradar:1 .`  Run: `docker run -p 8000:8000 reviewradar:1`.
Use the **exec form** `CMD ["a", "b"]` so signals reach your process and it stops cleanly.
Bind servers to `0.0.0.0` inside a container. `127.0.0.1` is reachable only from inside.

blocks.q: Which instruction runs a command while the image is being built?
blocks.why: `RUN` executes at build time. `CMD` runs when a container starts.

exercises.prompt: Put the Dockerfile lines in order for a FastAPI service.
hints: `FROM` is always the first instruction.
Copy the requirements file and install before copying all the code.
`CMD` is last.

exercises.prompt: Complete the Dockerfile.
hints: Two lines bring files into the image.
The last line says what to run when the container starts.
`COPY`, `COPY`, `CMD`.
exercises.template:
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
____ requirements.txt .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
____ . .
____ ["uvicorn", "main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0"]

exercises.prompt: What is the difference between an image and a container?
hints: Think class and object.
You can start many containers from one image.
The image is read-only; the container runs.
choices: An image is the packaged recipe result; a container is a running instance of it
A container is the file you build; an image is the running process
Images exist only in the cloud

exercises.prompt: A server inside your container binds to `127.0.0.1:8000`. From your laptop, `curl localhost:8000` (with `-p 8000:8000`) fails. Why?
hints: Where does `127.0.0.1` point inside a container?
Published ports reach the container from outside its own loopback.
choices: The app only accepts connections from inside the container; it should bind to `0.0.0.0`
Docker blocks all ports by default

concepts.title: Layers, caching and multi-stage builds
concepts.lede: Each instruction makes a cached layer. Order matters: put things that change rarely first, so rebuilds are fast and images stay small.

blocks.x: Tap a line to pretend you edited it. Everything from that line downwards is rebuilt. Compare the two Dockerfiles.

# Multi-stage: build with the heavy tools, ship only the result
FROM python:3.12 AS builder
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip wheel -r requirements.txt -w /wheels

FROM python:3.12-slim
COPY --from=builder /wheels /wheels
RUN pip install --no-index --find-links=/wheels /wheels/*.whl
COPY . /app
USER nobody                          # do not run as root
CMD ["python", "/app/main.py"]

x: A `.dockerignore` file (like `.gitignore`) keeps `.git`, virtual environments, caches and large data out of the build.
Pin versions: `python:3.12-slim`, not `python:latest`, so builds are repeatable.
Smaller images pull faster and have fewer vulnerabilities. Multi-stage builds and `-slim` bases help.

blocks.q: You edit one Python file. In the *requirements-first* Dockerfile, which layers rebuild?
blocks.why: Everything above the changed line stays cached, including the slow `pip install`.

exercises.prompt: Every code change makes this build wait for `pip install` again. Which line is the problem?
hints: Which layer changes on every edit?
Everything below a changed layer is rebuilt.
Copying all the code before installing invalidates the install layer.

explain.ask: In your own words: why does copying only requirements.txt first make rebuilds faster?
points: Docker caches each layer and reuses it if its inputs did not change
requirements.txt rarely changes, so the pip install layer stays cached when only code changes
explain.model: A layer is reused when its instruction and inputs are unchanged. The requirements file changes rarely, so the slow install stays cached. Code changes only invalidate the later `COPY . .` layer.

why: `CMD` would try to install at container start.
That only saves space; it does not fix the caching.

exercises.prompt: Complete the second stage so it uses files from the first stage.
hints: The first stage has a name after `AS`.
`--from=` refers to that name.
`builder`
exercises.template:
FROM python:3.12 AS builder
RUN pip wheel -r requirements.txt -w /wheels

FROM python:3.12-slim
COPY --from=____ /wheels /wheels

exercises.prompt: Which entries belong in `.dockerignore` for a ReviewRadar service? (Select all that apply.)
hints: Ignore what the image does not need.
The build still needs `requirements.txt`.
History, caches and large raw data only slow the build.

exercises.prompt: A security scan flags this Dockerfile for an unpinned base image. Which line is the problem?
hints: What does `latest` mean next month?
Builds should be repeatable.
Pin the version.

concepts.title: Kubernetes: Deployments and Pods
concepts.lede: You tell Kubernetes the state you want (three copies of this image) and it keeps reality matching. A Deployment manages identical Pods.

blocks.x:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: reviewradar-api
spec:
  replicas: 3                       # how many Pods
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: reviewradar-api          # which Pods this Deployment owns
  template:                         # the Pod blueprint
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: reviewradar-api        # MUST match the selector above
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: ghcr.io/arepaman/reviewradar:1.0
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8000
Labels are how Kubernetes connects things. A Service picks Pods by label. Toggle labels below to see which Pods match.

data.title: Which pods does the Service select?

x: **Pod**: one or more containers that run together. **Deployment**: keeps N identical Pods running and handles rolling updates. **ReplicaSet** does the counting underneath.
`kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml` sends the desired state. `kubectl get pods`, `kubectl logs <pod>`, `kubectl describe pod <pod>` show what is happening.
If a Pod dies, the Deployment makes a new one.

blocks.q: Which part of a Deployment must match the Pod template's labels?
blocks.why: The selector decides which Pods the Deployment manages.

exercises.prompt: Complete the start of a Deployment.
hints: Deployments belong to the `apps` API group.
The kind has a capital D.
`apps` and `Deployment`.
exercises.template:
apiVersion: ____/v1
kind: ____
metadata:
  name: reviewradar-api
spec:
  replicas: 3

exercises.prompt: The Deployment applies but creates no managed Pods (the API server rejects it). Which line is the problem?
hints: Compare the selector with the Pod template's labels.
They must agree.
`api` versus `web`.

choices: Make the template label `app: api` (matching the selector)

exercises.prompt: A Pod crashes. What does a Deployment with `replicas: 3` do?
hints: The Deployment holds the desired state.
It reconciles actual state toward desired state.
A new Pod is created.
choices: Creates a replacement Pod to get back to 3

concepts.title: Kubernetes: Services, config, probes and resources
concepts.lede: A Service gives Pods a stable address. ConfigMaps and Secrets inject settings. Probes and resource limits keep the cluster healthy.

blocks.x:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: reviewradar-api
spec:
  type: ClusterIP                  # reachable inside the cluster
  selector:
    app: reviewradar-api           # Pods with this label receive traffic
  ports:
    - port: 80                     # the Service's port
      targetPort: 8000             # the container's port
---
# inside the container spec of the Deployment:
resources:
  requests: {cpu: "250m", memory: "256Mi"}   # what the scheduler reserves
  limits:   {cpu: "500m", memory: "512Mi"}   # the hard ceiling
readinessProbe:                    # only send traffic when this succeeds
  httpGet: {path: /health, port: 8000}
livenessProbe:                     # restart the container if this keeps failing
  httpGet: {path: /health, port: 8000}
envFrom:
  - configMapRef: {name: api-config}
  - secretRef: {name: api-secrets}

x: **Readiness** controls whether a Pod gets traffic. **Liveness** controls whether it is restarted.
Memory units matter: `512Mi` is mebibytes, but `512` is **512 bytes**. CPU `250m` is a quarter of a core.
A **Secret** is only base64-encoded, not encrypted. Restrict access to it and prefer an external secret store.

blocks.q: Which probe decides whether a Pod receives traffic?
blocks.why: A failing readiness probe removes the Pod from the Service without restarting it.

exercises.prompt: Complete the Service so traffic on port 80 reaches the container's port 8000.
hints: `port` is what the Service listens on.
Another field names the container's port.
`targetPort`
exercises.template:
kind: Service
spec:

  ports:

exercises.prompt: A Pod keeps being killed immediately after it starts, with `OOMKilled`. Which line is the problem?
hints: Look at the memory unit.
A bare number means bytes.
512 bytes is not enough for a Python process.

why: Quotes do not change the unit; it is still bytes.
`m` means milli, so this is half a byte.

exercises.prompt: The app takes 40 seconds to load its model. Without a readiness probe, what goes wrong?
hints: When does Kubernetes start sending traffic by default?
As soon as the container is running.
A readiness probe delays traffic until the app answers.
choices: Traffic reaches the Pod before it is ready, so requests fail
The Pod is restarted every 5 seconds

exercises.prompt: A Kubernetes Secret holds a database password. Which statement is true?
hints: Base64 is an encoding, not encryption.
Anyone who can read the Secret object can decode it.
Use RBAC and, ideally, an external secret store.
choices: It is encrypted by default everywhere
It is only base64-encoded, so access must be restricted
It cannot be read by Pods

concepts.title: Terraform: HCL basics
concepts.lede: Terraform describes infrastructure as code. You declare what should exist; Terraform works out how to get there and records what it built.

x: Read inputs as `var.name`, resources as `<type>.<name>.<attribute>`, locals as `local.name`.
Workflow: `terraform init` (download providers), `terraform plan` (preview changes), `terraform apply` (make them), `terraform destroy` (remove).
**State** (`terraform.tfstate`) maps your code to real resources. Treat it as sensitive.

blocks.x: Always read the `plan` before `apply`. A line starting with `-/+` means the resource will be destroyed and recreated.

choices: Shows what would change, without changing anything
blocks.why: It compares your code with the real infrastructure and previews the difference.

exercises.prompt: Complete the input variable and use it.
hints: Inputs are declared with a block keyword.
They are read with a short prefix.
`variable` and `var`.

exercises.prompt: `terraform validate` fails on this resource. Which line is the problem?
hints: How are input variables referenced?
The block is `variable`, but the reference uses a shorter name.
It is `var.bucket_name`.

exercises.prompt: `terraform plan` shows `-/+ aws_db_instance.main (must be replaced)`. What should you do before applying?
hints: `-/+` means destroy then create.
Is that acceptable for this resource?
Investigate first, back up data if needed.
choices: Check what forces the replacement; destroying a database could lose data

concepts.title: Terraform on AWS: buckets, security and state
concepts.lede: A few AWS building blocks cover ReviewRadar: S3 for model files, IAM for permissions, security groups for network rules. Security mistakes here are costly.

x: **Least privilege**: give an IAM role only the actions and resources it needs (for example read-only access to one bucket).
Never open SSH (22) or databases to `0.0.0.0/0`. Restrict to your office or a VPN range.
Keep state **remote** (S3) with **locking** (DynamoDB) so two people cannot apply at once. Never commit `.tfstate` or `.tfvars` with secrets.

blocks.x: Mark secret outputs and variables `sensitive = true`, but remember state still contains them. Protect the state bucket.

blocks.q: Which IAM policy follows least privilege for a service that only reads models?
blocks.why: Only the needed action, on the needed resource.

exercises.prompt: Turn on versioning for the models bucket.
hints: Reference the bucket created above through one of its attributes.
The status is a capitalised word.
`id` and `Enabled`.

exercises.prompt: A security review rejects this security group. Which line is the problem?
hints: Who should be able to reach a database?
`0.0.0.0/0` means the entire internet.
Restrict it to the app's security group or a private CIDR.

choices: Limit the source to the app's private network (for example `10.0.0.0/16`) or its security group

exercises.prompt: Your team of three runs `terraform apply` from laptops. What setup avoids corrupted state?
hints: State must be shared and only one apply can run at a time.
Local files diverge.
A locking backend prevents simultaneous applies.
choices: Remote state in S3 with DynamoDB locking

concepts.title: Terraform: modules, loops and data sources
concepts.lede: Modules package reusable infrastructure. `for_each` creates many similar resources, and data sources read things that already exist.

x: `count` numbers resources 0, 1, 2. **Removing one from the middle shifts the rest and can destroy resources.**
`for_each` keys resources by name, so removing one affects only that one. Prefer it for collections.
`terraform plan -out=tfplan` then `terraform apply tfplan` applies exactly what you reviewed.
`lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }` protects critical resources.

blocks.q: You manage 3 buckets with `count` and remove the middle name from the list. What happens?
choices: Only the middle bucket is destroyed
Later buckets shift index and Terraform may destroy and recreate them
Terraform asks which one to keep
blocks.why: With `count`, resources are tracked by position.

exercises.prompt: Why is `for_each = toset(var.names)` usually safer than `count = length(var.names)` for a list of resources?
hints: What identifies each resource in state?
With `count` it is the index.
With `for_each` it is the key.
choices: Resources are tracked by name, so removing one does not shift the others

exercises.prompt: Use the module's output in another resource.
hints: The reference starts with `module.` and then the module's label.
The label is in quotes on the first line.
`vpc`

exercises.prompt: You want to apply exactly the changes you reviewed, even if someone edits the code afterwards. What do you run?
hints: A saved plan is a fixed set of actions.
Apply it by file name.
That is the reviewed-plan workflow used in CI/CD.
